opus-5.5.text:
I think what we're seeing is partly a natural consequence of where the field is right now. For a few years, the dominant story was scaling: more data, more compute, bigger models. That story produced remarkable results, but it also concentrated the frontier in a handful of very large organizations, because only they could afford to play that game. What's changed recently is that many people, including researchers inside those big labs, have started to feel that pure scaling alone is hitting diminishing returns, or at least that it isn't the only path forward. And when the direction becomes less certain, that's exactly when you see new labs appear.

So I'd read this wave less as "everyone wants to build another big model" and more as people betting on different hypotheses. Some focus on reasoning and reinforcement learning, some on world models or embodied intelligence, some on efficiency, and some, like the direction I care about, on interpretability and on making AI more scientific, building models whose internal structure we can actually understand, and using AI to help do science itself.

In the US, a lot of these labs are founded by people who left the big companies with a specific conviction and enough credibility to raise money around it. In China, there's a somewhat different flavor. There's strong engineering talent and a lot of momentum after open-weight models showed you can get very far with clever engineering and limited compute. Constraints actually force creativity. When you can't simply buy more GPUs, you have to think harder about algorithms, data efficiency, and architecture.

Personally, I think this diversity is healthy. Science advances when many groups explore different directions in parallel, rather than everyone climbing the same hill. Most of these labs won't become giants, and that's fine. What matters is whether some of them find genuinely new ideas, the kind of conceptual breakthroughs that the next phase of AI will need. I'm cautiously optimistic, but I'd also say the real test is a few years out: which labs are doing research that's truly different, and which are just repackaging the same recipe with a new name.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the first thing to say is that these labs are a symptom, not a cause. The cause is that for the first time in maybe a decade, the frontier is no longer owned by a handful of players who have already figured out the recipe. Scaling pretraining got us very far, but everyone now senses that the next big step is not going to come from just doing the same thing with ten times more compute. And when the recipe is uncertain, the barrier to entry drops in a strange way. You no longer need to be OpenAI or Google to have a credible shot, because the question is not "who can execute the known plan best" but "who can find the next plan."

So you see all these new labs, and if you look closely, almost every one of them is a bet on a specific thesis. Some bet on new architectures, some bet on reasoning and post-training, some bet on agents, some bet on interpretability as a path to better models rather than just safer ones. I find that healthy. In physics, the periods of fastest progress were always the ones where many small groups were trying different directions, not the ones where everyone converged on one approach.

There is a difference between the two countries, though, and I don't think it's just about chips or money. In the US, the new labs are often founded by people who left big labs with a disagreement, either a scientific disagreement or a cultural one. They are saying "the big lab is doing it wrong, here is how I would do it." That gives them a clear identity from day one. In China, a lot of the energy is coming from a different place: a combination of very strong engineering talent, a constraint on compute that actually forces creativity, and a sense that if you can do it cheaper and more efficiently, that is itself a frontier. DeepSeek showed the world that efficiency can be a form of leadership, and I think that changed how many young Chinese researchers think about what's possible.

What I personally pay attention to is not the valuation or the headlines but whether a lab has a real scientific question it is trying to answer. A lab that is just "we will also train a big model" will probably not survive, because the big labs will always have more resources. A lab that says "we think intelligence works like this, and we are going to test it" can win even if it is small, because if the idea is right, the idea compounds.

My one worry is the opposite of what people usually worry about. People worry there are too many labs. I worry that many of them look different on the surface but are converging on the same ideas underneath, chasing the same benchmarks and hiring from the same pool. If that happens, we get the appearance of diversity without the substance. The thing that would make me most optimistic is seeing labs that are genuinely weird, trying things that look wrong to most people, because that is historically where the real breakthroughs come from.

astra-6.text:
I think it reflects a shared belief that AI is still open enough for a new team to make a meaningful contribution. If everyone believed the core questions had been settled and the winners were already determined, there would be much less reason to start a lab.

But I would separate two motivations. One is that people see a large commercial opportunity. The other is that researchers have a different view of how intelligence should be built, and they want the freedom to pursue it. Those motivations can coexist, but they lead to different choices about hiring, compute, and how quickly you need to release products.

I’m cautious about treating China and the United States as two internally uniform groups. A small research team may have more in common with a small team in the other country than with a large company at home. The useful question is: what can this particular lab explore that an existing organization would struggle to explore?

So I see the wave as encouraging, but the number of labs is not itself a measure of progress. The real test is whether they produce different ideas. If everyone follows the same recipe, we get more competition around one approach. If some teams can afford to question the recipe, we have a better chance of discovering something new.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d look at it through two questions: why start a new lab now, and what can a small team do differently from a large organization?

AI is still young enough that there isn’t one settled recipe for progress. People have different intuitions about what matters—scaling, reasoning, learning from the physical world, or finding better ways to represent knowledge. A new lab gives a team the freedom to pursue one of those intuitions seriously.

At the same time, there’s a tension. It’s easier to start experimenting, but competing at the frontier can require enormous resources. So the important question is whether a new lab has a distinct scientific direction, or simply wants to do what the existing labs are doing with fewer resources.

I’d apply that same question to both China and the United States. The national comparison is interesting, but I’m more interested in whether these labs create room for different ideas. If they all converge on the same approach, having more labs doesn’t necessarily mean more discovery. If some can take risks and challenge assumptions, then this wave could be very valuable.
